sound
of metallic hooves on the ground, rather than on the
image
of a horse.
The introduction of this episode is interpreted as a musical
overture

children: This initial disjointed section of
Sirens
has numerous sounds, musicality and musical allusions.

The short phrases, compound words and sounds introduce the ‘Fuga per Canonem’ technique Joyce employs, although the reader may not be fully aware of it before completing the episode. Joyce stated ‘It is a fugue with all musical notations: piano, forte, rallentando, and so on’, (Ellmann p459).
The fugal elements are :
Subject : the Siren’s song
Answer : Mr. Bloom’s entry and monologue
Counter-subject : Boylan
Divertimenti : Songs of Ben Dollard and Mr Bloom
(Gilbert, S. James Joyce’s Ulysses).
Idolores
refers to a character in an 1899 opera:
Florodora
(spelt Floradora in Gifford p291).

6757353.twitter_share_message: “Bloom is being truly emasculated in this section. ‘Pwee! Little wind piped wee.’ Wee in Scottish…” —@Genius

children: Bloom is being truly emasculated in this section. ‘Pwee! Little wind piped wee.’ Wee in Scottish dialect which has influenced Northern Ireland, means small. Here the little wind piped wee, alludes to a wind instrument, following on from the musical theme, Joyce refers frequently to wind instruments throughout the chapter, like the fife. Pwee is the noise the wind pipe makes. But as usual Joyce is employing ‘double entendre’ and here the little wind pipe also alludes to BLoom’s small phallus. The idea is further reinforced in the next section when Joyce speaks of ‘True men…Like you men. Will lift your tschink with tschunk.’ i.e. they are real men, men that women like Molly desire and would in Bloom’s mind be potential suitors for his unfaithful wife, because they are able to perform the deed with gusto and possess virile attributes that Leopold does not have, like chunky sized phalluses. Joyce  alludes to this when he says ‘they can lift women up with their 'tschunk.’

Joyce deliberately chooses to emasculate Bloom the main character of this book in contrast to Ulysses in the Odyssey, Bloom is not depicted as strong, manly and vigorous but instead meek, cuckolded and not well endowed. Joyce is creating a true anti-hero in every sense of the word. From the description of Bloom’s small penis to his toilet habits and the derisory comments of others, we are constantly invited to scrutinize Bloom.
